steps.title: Tu or Lei greetings
steps.how_to: How to greet and stop people with the friendly tu or the polite Lei.
steps.intro: Italian has a friendly way and a polite way to say 'you'. You'll use them to greet friends, shopkeepers and strangers, and to get someone's attention.
steps.notice: With friends you say 'Come stai?' and 'Senti, scusa'. With shopkeepers and strangers you say 'Come sta?' and 'Senta, scusi'. If you're unsure, 'Salve!' is safe with anyone.

ask.en: Hi! How are you?
Good morning, how are you?

ask.it: Un signore anziano passa. Cosa dici per fermarlo?
ask.en: An older man walks by. What do you say to stop him?

mission.goal: Greet the shopkeeper politely and ask how they are

steps.title: Say how you are
steps.how_to: How to say how you are and ask the other person back.
steps.intro: After 'How are you?' you'll want to answer and ask in return. This is what you say in a shop, on the stairs or anywhere you chat.
steps.notice: To say how you are, Italian uses 'sto': 'Sto bene, grazie.' Then you hand the question back with 'E Lei?' or 'E tu?'.

ask.en: How are you? (polite)
Hi! How are you?
Good morning! How are you?

answer.it: Non c'è male, grazie. E Lei?

mission.goal: Tell a neighbour you're well and ask how they are

steps.title: Greetings by time of day
steps.how_to: How to pick buongiorno or buonasera for the time of day.
steps.intro: You'll greet people every time you walk into a shop or bar. Here is how to choose the right greeting for the hour.
steps.notice: Buongiorno works until lunch or early afternoon. Buonasera takes over from mid-afternoon, much earlier than English 'good evening'. Buonanotte is only for when someone is going to bed.
steps.context: Italians greet when they walk into a shop or bar, and Buonasera starts surprisingly early, around 3 or 4 p.m.

ask.it: Sono le dieci. Entri in un bar. Cosa dici?
ask.en: It's ten o'clock. You walk into a bar. What do you say?

ask.it: Sono le cinque. Entri in farmacia. Cosa dici?
ask.en: It's five o'clock. You walk into a pharmacy. What do you say?

ask.it: Sono le nove di sera. Entri in un bar. Cosa dici?
ask.en: It's nine in the evening. You walk into a bar. What do you say?

mission.goal: Greet the barista with the right greeting for the time of day

steps.title: Saying goodbye well
steps.how_to: How to say goodbye and answer a good wish.
steps.intro: When you leave a shop or meet a neighbour again, you'll say goodbye with a good wish. You'll also answer one when you get it.

examples.it: Grazie, anche a te! Ci vediamo!

steps.notice: In the day you wish 'Buona giornata', in the evening 'Buona serata'. You answer 'Altrettanto!', or 'Anche a Lei!' (polite) or 'Anche a te!' (friendly). 'A domani!' and 'Ci vediamo!' are for people you'll see again.
steps.context: Italians say goodbye when they leave a shop or bar, and walking out in silence comes across as rude.

ask.it: Esci dal negozio la mattina. Cosa dici?
ask.en: You leave a shop in the morning. What do you say?

ask.it: Il negoziante dice: Buona giornata! Tu rispondi?
ask.en: The shopkeeper says: Have a good day! What do you answer?

ask.it: Un amico dice: Buona serata! Tu rispondi?
ask.en: A friend says: Have a nice evening! What do you answer?

answer.it: Grazie, anche a te! Ci vediamo!

mission.goal: Say goodbye with a good wish as you leave

steps.title: Saying you didn't understand
steps.how_to: How to say you missed something, and tell people when you've got it.
steps.intro: Here you'll learn to say you didn't catch what someone said, and to say "got it" when you do. You'll use it at any counter or in any chat that moves too fast.

examples.en: I only speak a little Italian.

steps.notice: For something someone has just said, the phrases are ho capito and non ho capito, with non right before ho. Use them as two ready-made phrases.
steps.context: Most people are pleased that you're trying, so telling them you only speak a little Italian goes down well.

ask.en: Did you understand?

ask.it: Sono quattro euro e cinquanta. Ha capito?
ask.en: That's four euros fifty. Did you understand?
Do you speak Italian?

answer.en: I only speak a little Italian.

mission.goal: Tell the shopkeeper you didn't catch the price.

steps.title: Asking someone to repeat
steps.how_to: How to ask someone politely to repeat or to speak more slowly.
steps.intro: Now you'll be able to ask people to say it again, or more slowly. You'll use it whenever a price or an answer goes by too fast.
steps.notice: Può and a basic verb together make a polite request, with nothing in between: può ripetere. With a friend, say puoi ripetere.
steps.context: Many people speed up or switch to English, so a friendly "più piano, per favore" is normal and expected.

ask.it: Come chiede di ripetere, in modo cortese?
ask.en: How do you politely ask someone to repeat?

ask.it: Come chiede di parlare più piano?
ask.en: How do you ask someone to speak more slowly?

ask.it: E con un amico, come chiede di ripetere?
ask.en: And with a friend, how do you ask them to repeat?

mission.goal: Ask the ticket clerk to repeat and slow down.

steps.title: Asking about a word
steps.how_to: How to ask what a word means, how to say it in Italian, and how to spell it.
steps.intro: You'll learn three short questions for words you don't know. They help in a shop, at a bar, or anywhere a new word comes up.

examples.en: How do you say “receipt” in Italian?

steps.notice: Cosa vuol dire asks what a word means, come si dice asks for the Italian word, and come si scrive asks for the spelling. Each one is complete as it stands, with no extra word.

ask.en: How do you ask what “scontrino” means?

ask.it: Come chiede la parola italiana per “receipt”?
ask.en: How do you ask for the Italian word for “receipt”?

answer.en: How do you say “receipt” in Italian?

ask.en: And how do you ask for the spelling?

mission.goal: Ask the shopkeeper how to say a word in Italian.

say.it: Scusi, come si dice “receipt” in italiano?
say.en: Excuse me, how do you say “receipt” in Italian?

steps.title: Say your name
steps.how_to: How to give your name and ask for theirs.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say your name and ask for someone else's. You'd use it the first time you meet a neighbour or a classmate.

examples.it: Mi chiamo Rosa. E Lei, come si chiama?
examples.en: My name's Rosa. And what's your name?

examples.it: Mi chiamo Marco. E tu, come ti chiami?
examples.en: My name's Marco. And what's your name?
Nice to meet you, I'm Rosa. What's your name?
My name's Tom. Nice to meet you!

steps.notice: Mi chiamo and your name is the whole sentence. Ask with come si chiama for an older person or a stranger, and come ti chiami for a friend or classmate. Add piacere when you hear the name.

ask.en: What's your name?

ask.it: Mi chiamo Magda. E Lei, come si chiama?
ask.en: My name's Magda. And what's your name?

answer.en: My name's …. Nice to meet you!

ask.en: What's your name, excuse me?

answer.en: My name's …, nice to meet you.

mission.goal: Tell a neighbour your name and ask for theirs

say.it: Mi chiamo …. E Lei, come si chiama?
say.en: My name's …. And what's your name?

steps.title: Say where you're from
steps.how_to: How to say your nationality and your city, and ask the same back.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say where you're from and ask someone else. People ask this early in almost every first chat.

examples.it: Sono americano, di Denver. E tu, di dove sei?
examples.en: I'm American, from Denver. And where are you from?

steps.notice: Sono and your nationality, then di and your city. A man says americano and a woman says americana. Ask di dove sei with tu and di dov'è with Lei.
steps.context: Di dove sei? is one of the first things Italians ask, because where you come from matters a lot here.

ask.en: Where are you from?
Where are you from? (Lei)

answer.en: I'm American, from …. (a woman says americana)

ask.en: Are you English?

answer.en: No, I'm American, from …. (a woman says americana)

mission.goal: Say where you're from and ask a classmate the same

say.it: Sono americano, di …. E tu, di dove sei?
say.en: I'm American, from …. And where are you from?

steps.title: Say where you live
steps.how_to: How to say you live here and not just on holiday.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say that you live here and where. You'd use it when someone asks if you're on holiday.

examples.en: And are you here on holiday?
I live here, in Mazzini Street.
Where do you live? I live in Florence.

steps.notice: Abito means I live. Say abito qui for here, in via and the street, or a and a city. Ask dove abita with Lei and dove abiti with tu.
steps.context: Saying you live here, not that you're on holiday, changes the conversation: people start treating you as a neighbour.

ask.en: Where do you live? (tu)
Are you here on holiday?
Where do you live? (Lei)

mission.goal: Tell someone you live here, not on holiday

steps.title: Say how long and why
steps.how_to: How to say how long you've been here and why you came.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say how long you've been in Italy and why you're here. You'd use it when someone asks about your stay.

examples.it: Sono in Italia da tre settimane.
examples.en: I've been in Italy for three weeks.
I've been studying Italian for a month.

steps.notice: Say sono qui per and what you want to do to give the reason. For how long you've been here, say da and the time: sono in Italia da tre settimane.

ask.en: Are you here for work?

answer.it: No, sono qui per imparare l'italiano.
answer.en: No, I'm here to learn Italian.

ask.en: Are you here on holiday?

answer.it: No, sono in Italia da … settimane.
answer.en: No, I've been in Italy for … weeks.

ask.en: Are you studying Italian?

answer.it: Sì, studio l'italiano da un mese.
answer.en: Yes, I've been studying Italian for a month.

mission.goal: Tell a classmate why you're here and for how long

say.it: Sono qui per imparare l'italiano. Sono in Italia da tre settimane.
say.en: I'm here to learn Italian. I've been in Italy for three weeks.

steps.title: Say what you do
steps.how_to: How to say your work or that you're retired, and understand a welcome.
steps.intro: You'll be able to say what you do and understand when people welcome you. You'd use it when a new acquaintance asks about your life here.
steps.notice: Sono in pensione says you're retired. Lavoro come and your job says what you do. Ben arrivato is welcome to a man and ben arrivata to a woman.
steps.context: If people compliment your Italian, you can just say Grazie, ma sto imparando!

ask.en: Are you retired?
Are you here for work?

ask.it: Ben arrivato! Sei qui per lavoro?
ask.en: Welcome! Are you here for work?

mission.goal: Tell a neighbour what you do

say.en: I work as a …. And you?

steps.title: Asking for a drink
steps.how_to: How to ask for one drink or snack with the right word for "a".
steps.intro: Let's start with the simplest order: one coffee, one juice, one spritz. You'll use this every time you step up to the counter.
steps.notice: Most words take un, but uno goes before s plus a consonant, and una or un' go with feminine words. Learn each word with its little word, and for a milky coffee ask for un latte macchiato.
steps.context: Un caffè always means an espresso.

ask.en: An espresso or a cappuccino?
A fresh juice or an orangeade?

ask.it: Un cornetto o un latte macchiato?
ask.en: A croissant or a latte macchiato?

mission.goal: Order a spritz at the counter.

steps.title: Ordering for two
steps.how_to: How to order more than one of the same thing.
steps.intro: When you're with a friend, you'll ask for two of something. Here is how the words change for two coffees, two croissants or two juices.

examples.it: Due cappuccini e due cornetti, per favore.
examples.en: Two cappuccinos and two croissants, please.

examples.it: Due tè e due spritz, per favore.
examples.en: Two teas and two spritzes, please.

steps.notice: Words ending in -o change to -i, and words ending in -a change to -e. Words ending in an accented vowel or a consonant stay the same: due caffè, due spritz.

ask.en: How many espressos, one or two?
Cappuccinos or fresh juices?
Two teas or two spritzes?

mission.goal: Order two espressos at the counter.

steps.title: Saying I'd like
steps.how_to: How to ask politely with vorrei or per me.
steps.intro: Here are two polite ways to start an order. You can use them for anything, from a juice to a glass of water.

examples.en: I'd like a fresh orange juice.

examples.it: Vorrei un bicchiere d'acqua, per favore.
examples.en: I'd like a glass of water, please.

examples.it: Per me un cappuccino e un cornetto.
examples.en: A cappuccino and a croissant for me.

steps.notice: Vorrei means "I'd like" and sounds polite at any counter. Per me plus the item works too, and so does the item plus per favore.
steps.context: Cappuccino is a morning drink; after lunch Italians order an espresso.

ask.en: Good morning! What can I get you?
Yes? What can I get you?

answer.it: Per me un cappuccino e un cornetto.
answer.en: A cappuccino and a croissant for me.

ask.en: Good evening! What can I get you?

answer.it: Vorrei un bicchiere d'acqua, per favore.
answer.en: I'd like a glass of water, please.

mission.goal: Ask politely for a fresh orange juice.

say.en: I'd like a fresh orange juice.

steps.title: Saying what you're having
steps.how_to: How to say what you're having and ask a friend the same.
steps.intro: In Italy you "take" your coffee, so one little verb covers it. You'll use it to say what you're having and to ask someone else.
steps.notice: Prendo means "I'll have" when you order. Ask a friend Cosa prendi? and someone you address formally Cosa prende?

ask.en: What are you having?
What are you having? (formal)

ask.it: Io prendo un caffè. E tu?
ask.en: I'm having an espresso. And you?

mission.goal: Ask a friend what they're having.

steps.title: Answering the barista
steps.how_to: How to understand the barista's questions and answer them.
steps.intro: The barista will often give you two choices. Once you know these questions, you can answer quickly with just one word and grazie.

examples.en: Yes? What can I get you?
At the counter or at a table?

examples.it: Il cornetto semplice o alla crema?

steps.notice: Each question offers two choices, so answer with the one you want and add grazie. If you're treating a friend, say Offro io!
steps.context: Standing at the banco is cheaper than sitting at a table.

ask.en: Still or sparkling?

ask.it: Il cornetto semplice o alla crema?
ask.en: Plain croissant or with custard?
At the counter or at a table?

answer.en: At the counter, thanks. It's on me!

mission.goal: Ask for a glass of water and say still.

steps.title: Numbers up to thousands
steps.how_to: How to say and understand numbers, from twenty to two thousand.
steps.intro: You'll be able to hear and say prices like twenty-one or two hundred euros. You'll need this at every till, ticket window and market stall.
steps.notice: Numbers are built just like in English, but the tens lose their last vowel before uno and otto: ventuno, ventotto, trentuno. Ventitré and trentatré take an accent. For thousands, say mille, then duemila.

ask.it: Quanto costa il biglietto? Sono 21 euro.
ask.en: How much is the ticket? It's 21 euros.

ask.it: Quanto costa la borsa? Dica 28 euro.
ask.en: How much is the bag? Say 28 euros.

ask.it: Quanto costa il tavolo? Dica 2000 euro.
ask.en: How much is the table? Say 2,000 euros.

mission.goal: Ask the price of a ticket and listen for the number.

steps.title: Understanding prices in euro
steps.how_to: How to understand a spoken price in euros and cents.
steps.intro: You'll be able to follow what the cashier says when they tell you the price. You'll hear it every time you pay at the bar, the bakery or a shop.
steps.notice: Euro stays the same whether it's one or many: un euro, due euro. The number after e is the cents, and people often leave the word out.

ask.en: How much is the newspaper?
How much is the espresso?
How much is the bread?

mission.goal: Ask the price of the bread and listen for the euros.

steps.title: Asking how much
steps.how_to: How to ask the price of one thing, several things, or the total.
steps.intro: You'll be able to ask what something costs, and what your whole order comes to. You'll say it at the market, in a shop or at the bar till.

examples.it: Un caffè e un cornetto. Quant'è?
examples.en: An espresso and a croissant. How much is that?

steps.notice: Say costa for one thing and costano for several, with the thing you're asking about coming after. To ask about the whole order, say Quant'è?

ask.it: Un pane: come chiedi il prezzo?
ask.en: One loaf: how do you ask the price?

ask.it: Le pesche: come chiedi il prezzo?
ask.en: The peaches: how do you ask the price?

ask.it: Un caffè e un cornetto: come chiedi il totale?
ask.en: An espresso and a croissant: how do you ask the total?

mission.goal: Ask the price of some peaches.

steps.title: Paying by card or cash
steps.how_to: How to ask to pay by card or say you'll pay cash.
steps.intro: You'll be able to ask if you can pay by card, or say you'll pay cash and hand over the money. You'll say it at the till of any bar, bakery or shop.

examples.it: Pago in contanti. Ecco a Lei.
examples.en: I'll pay cash. Here you are.

steps.notice: After Posso, use pagare, just like that. When you hand over the money, say Ecco a Lei, or just Ecco.
steps.context: Small shops and market stalls still prefer cash for small amounts, so Pago in contanti is a very useful thing to say.

ask.it: Vuoi pagare con la carta. Che cosa chiedi?
ask.en: You want to pay by card. What do you ask?

ask.it: Vuoi pagare in contanti. Che cosa dici?
ask.en: You want to pay cash. What do you say?

ask.it: Dai i soldi alla cassiera. Che cosa dici?
ask.en: You hand the money to the cashier. What do you say?

mission.goal: Ask to pay by card at the till.

steps.title: Talking about change
steps.how_to: How to answer when the cashier asks if you have change.
steps.intro: You'll be able to understand when someone asks for coins, and tell them politely that you have none. You'll need it when you pay with a big note.

examples.en: Sorry, I haven't got any change.

examples.it: Va bene. Ecco il resto: otto euro.
examples.en: That's fine. Here's your change: eight euros.

steps.notice: Ha moneta? and Ha spiccioli? ask the same thing. If you have no coins, say Mi dispiace, non ho spiccioli. When you get your change, take the scontrino, the receipt, too.
steps.context: Cashiers often ask Ha moneta? to avoid breaking a big note.

ask.en: Have you got any change?

answer.en: Sorry, I haven't got any change.

ask.en: Have you got any coins?

answer.it: Mi dispiace, non ho spiccioli. Ecco a Lei.
answer.en: Sorry, I haven't got any change. Here you are.

ask.it: Ecco il resto e lo scontrino.
ask.en: Here's your change and the receipt.

mission.goal: Pay for a newspaper with a ten-euro note and say you have no change.

say.en: Sorry, I haven't got any change.
